rationale: Start with a broad, fairly strong scouting gradient at mid temperature to elute all 10 compounds within the time window while revealing the overall retention spread and any severe compression. This gives a safe first map of where the mixture sits before optimizing slope, window, and temperature.

All pairs are already fully resolved, so the only available gain is reducing analysis time. Keep the same window and temperature and shorten the gradient one step to see how much faster we can go before any pair drops below baseline target resolution.

The current method is close to the 10 min target and the critical pair is still just above R = 1.5, so another small reduction in gradient time is the most direct test for a higher CRF. This probes whether we can bring the last peak under 10 min without sacrificing the weakest separation.

At 14 min the run is fast enough, and the only loss is the marginal 6/7 pair. Lowering temperature one step should increase retention and often improves selectivity/resolution for close pairs, with only a modest risk of pushing the last peak back above 10 min.

Lowering temperature hurt selectivity by collapsing a different pair, so test the opposite direction at the same fast gradient. A 45 C run may restore or improve the critical mid-cluster spacing while keeping the last peak under 10 min.

Temperature moves worsened selectivity, so keep 40 C and instead slightly narrow the high-organic end to flatten the gradient around the late-eluting cluster. This may recover the weak 6/7 resolution while still keeping the run fast enough to stay near or under 10 min.

Reducing phi1 from 0.95 to 0.90 improved the critical pair substantially while keeping all peaks before 10 min, so continue one more step in the same direction. This should further flatten the gradient in the congested region and may push the 6/7 pair to full credit.

At phi1 = 0.85 the critical pair reaches full credit, so the next move is to shorten the gradient and try to pull the last peak back under 10 min. This tests whether the gained selectivity margin is enough to tolerate a steeper, faster run.

The 12 min gradient at phi1 = 0.85 became too steep for the critical pair, while phi1 = 0.90 at 14 min was very close to optimal. Testing phi1 = 0.90 with tG = 12 checks whether a slightly wider high-end window can recover just enough time advantage without losing too much resolution.

We know 14 min, 0.90 gives the best balance so far and that resolution improves as the gradient is made shallower; moving to 16 min should push the critical pair to full credit. This tests whether the gain in resolution outweighs the small time penalty and may surpass the current best CRF.

The best region is clearly near 14 min and 40 C, so now probe the other end of the window by raising phi0 one step while keeping phi1 and tG fixed. This slightly narrows the gradient span and may preserve enough selectivity around the critical cluster while pulling the whole chromatogram earlier for a higher CRF.

Injection 11 is very close to ideal, missing only a little resolution on the 6/7 pair; lowering phi1 by one step should flatten the gradient in that crowded region and may push that pair to full credit. The expected retention increase is modest, so this has a good chance to reach CRF 1.000 or very near it.

You have reached the maximum observed CRF, so the only worthwhile remaining search is for a potentially more robust method that still scores 1.000 while moving the last peak slightly earlier. Raising phi0 one step keeps the successful high-end window but narrows the span further, which may retain full resolution and bring t_last just under 10 min.

The last move kept full resolution and shifted the chromatogram earlier, so continue increasing phi0 one step to see whether a still narrower window preserves the 1.5 minimum while further shortening retention. This is the most direct way to map the fast edge of the 1.000-CRF plateau.

phi0 = 0.15, phi1 = 0.85 gave a robust 1.000 score, while increasing phi0 further lost critical-pair resolution. Lowering phi1 one step from that robust point should slightly flatten the gradient in the crowded region and may keep full resolution with a similar or only slightly later t_last.

The current 1.000-score plateau is around phi0 0.10–0.15, phi1 0.85, tG 14, and 40 C; to search for an even faster fully resolved method, test a shorter gradient while lowering temperature to recover selectivity on the critical 6/7 pair. This probes whether speed lost at 12 min can be offset by the favorable selectivity shift from cooler conditions.

Cooling at 12 min created a severe 5/6 collapse, so test the opposite temperature direction at the same fast geometry. This checks whether higher temperature can preserve the speed benefit while changing selectivity differently enough to keep the crowded middle region fully resolved.

With 14 min methods at phi0 0.10 and 0.15 already at CRF 1.000, the remaining useful search is robustness around that optimum. A 16 min version at phi0 0.10, phi1 0.85 should provide a stronger resolution safety margin for the critical pair and helps define the shallow side of the optimum plateau.

The 0.10/0.85/14/40 method already scores 1.000 with only a 0.01 min excess on the last peak, so a small further flattening of the upper end is worth checking. This tests whether lower phi1 can maintain full resolution while nudging the method onto a more robust 1.000 plateau or revealing the time limit more clearly.

You already have multiple 1.000 methods, so with the remaining budget it is useful to test temperature robustness around the best composition window. A 45 C run at the successful 0.10/0.85/14 setting will show whether the optimum is broad or whether 40 C is uniquely favorable for the critical mid-cluster selectivity.

Since 40 C is clearly best and both higher and lower temperatures can alter selectivity sharply, test the cooler side at the best-performing composition to complete the robustness map around the 1.000 plateau. This will confirm whether phi0 = 0.15, phi1 = 0.85 is uniquely optimal only at 40 C or tolerates some cooling.

The best methods are centered at 40 C and phi1 = 0.85, with phi0 = 0.10–0.15 both giving CRF 1.000; increasing phi1 one step from the best phi0 = 0.15 point will define the upper boundary of that optimum region. This checks whether the method can remain perfect with a slightly stronger final solvent while shortening the tail end.

The evidence shows 40 C is the sweet spot, but the lower-temperature boundary has only been checked at phi0 = 0.15. Testing 0.10/0.85/14 at 35 C completes the robustness picture around the other 1.000 method and confirms whether the same 5/6 selectivity collapse occurs there too.

With only two injections left and multiple 1.000 methods already found, the remaining value is to map robustness on the slower, high-resolution side near the best phi0 = 0.15 composition. A 16 min run at 0.15/0.80/40 C should provide a strong fully resolved benchmark and confirm the broadness of the optimum basin.

For the final run, map the remaining unexplored strong-end boundary adjacent to the best 1.000 region at 40 C. This will confirm how quickly the critical 6/7 pair deteriorates when phi1 is increased from the optimal 0.85–0.90 range.
